params.title: Antenna Systems
params.subtitle: The slotted waveguide array, transmission lines, sending the antenna's bearing to the display, and waveguides.

onScreen: Antenna Systems
Slotted array, transmission lines, bearing to the display, waveguides
scenes.narration: This lesson follows the radar signal from the transmitter up to the antenna. You'll learn how the slotted waveguide array forms its beam, how transmission lines and waveguides carry microwave energy with low loss, and how the antenna's position, its bearing, gets to the display. We'll begin with the antenna itself.

callouts.label: Slotted waveguide array: the most common type on commercial vessels
Precisely spaced slots cut in one wall of the waveguide
Each slot radiates a small share, forming a narrow horizontal beam
Compact and rugged: no separate feed horn needed
Has largely replaced the truncated parabolic reflectors of older sets

onScreen: Slotted waveguide array: most common on commercial vessels
Precisely spaced slots in one wall
Narrow horizontal beam
Compact, rugged, no separate feed horn
Replaced older truncated parabolic reflectors
scenes.narration: The typical shipboard radar antenna, and the most common type aboard commercial maritime vessels, is the slotted waveguide array. It's a length of waveguide with precisely spaced slots cut in one wall. Each slot radiates a small share of the energy, and together they form a narrow horizontal beam. The array is compact and rugged, and it needs no separate feed horn. Truncated parabolic reflectors were common on older sets, but the slotted waveguide array has largely replaced them.

params.title: Why the beam points a little off
items: End-fed array: each slot's phase is set by the guide wavelength
Change the transmitter frequency and the beam swings slightly: frequency scan
Frequency scan is also called beam squint
Main lobe center: several degrees off a line perpendicular to the antenna
Slots sit slightly off a half guide wavelength, so reflections don't build a high VSWR

onScreen: End-fed: slot phase set by guide wavelength
Frequency change swings the beam: frequency scan
Also called beam squint
Lobe center several degrees off perpendicular
Slot spacing keeps VSWR low
scenes.narration: The slotted array has a couple of quirks the exam asks about. First, an end-fed slotted waveguide array exhibits frequency scan. Each slot's phase is set by the guide wavelength, so changing the transmitter frequency swings the beam direction slightly. This is also called beam squint. Second, the center of the transmitted lobe is several degrees offset from a line perpendicular to the antenna. That's because the slots are spaced slightly off a half guide wavelength, so their small reflections don't add up to a high VSWR, or voltage standing wave ratio.

params.title: Bearing resolution and antenna length
labels: 2 targets at the same range, on slightly different bearings
Good bearing resolution depends on a narrow horizontal beam
Longer antenna, narrower beam: θ ≈ 70λ/L degrees; double L, halve θ
Vertical beam kept fairly wide, so targets stay in view as the ship rolls

onScreen: 2 targets at the same range, slightly different bearings
Narrow horizontal beam: good bearing resolution
θ ≈ 70λ/L degrees: double the length, halve the beamwidth
Vertical beam fairly wide for rolling
scenes.narration: Bearing resolution is the ability to separate 2 targets at the same range on slightly different bearings, like these. Good bearing resolution largely depends on a narrow antenna beam in the horizontal plane; a wide beam would paint both as one echo. The longer the antenna, the narrower the horizontal beamwidth. Beamwidth is inversely proportional to the antenna's length in wavelengths: roughly, theta equals 70 lambda over L, in degrees. So doubling the length roughly halves the beamwidth. The vertical beam is kept fairly wide, so targets stay in view as the ship rolls.

onScreen: Z sub O = √(L ÷ C)
scenes.narration: The impedance of a transmission line, Z sub O, is the square root of L over C: the ratio of inductance L to capacitance C. Convert both to base units, henries and farads, first. Worked example: a section of line has 250 microhenries of L and 1000 picofarads of C. 250 microhenries is 250 millionths of a henry. 1000 picofarads is 1 billionth of a farad. Divide, and you get 250,000. The square root of 250,000 is 500. So Z sub O is 500 ohms.

params.title: Standing waves on a mismatched line
labels: The forward wave travels toward the load
A load that doesn't match Z<sub>O</sub> reflects part of it
Forward and reflected waves form standing waves
Load equal to Z<sub>O</sub>: no standing waves

onScreen: Forward wave toward the load
Mismatched load reflects part of it
Standing waves: energy not absorbed by the load
Load equal to Z sub O: no standing waves
scenes.narration: What do standing waves on a transmission line tell you? That some of the energy is not absorbed by the load. The forward wave travels toward the load. If the load doesn't match Z sub O, part of the forward wave reflects back. The forward and reflected waves combine into standing waves along the line. Terminate the line in an impedance equal to Z sub O, and the load absorbs the energy: there are no standing waves.

blocks.label: Power meter
blocks.note: Reads the forward and reflected samples

onScreen: Dual directional coupler samples forward and reflected power
Power meter reads the samples
Network analyzer measures the reflection
Spectrum analyzer alone: only frequencies and levels
scenes.narration: How might you measure the VSWR of a microwave transmission line device? With a dual directional coupler, a power meter and a network analyzer. The transmitter's signal passes through the dual directional coupler to the device. The coupler samples both the forward and the reflected power, and the power meter reads those samples. A network analyzer measures the reflection directly. A spectrum analyzer alone won't do the job: it shows only frequencies and signal levels.

params.title: Line and waveguide good practice
items: Z<sub>O</sub> is set by construction: conductor size, spacing and dielectric
Not by length: cut a 72 Ω line at its center and each half is still 72 Ω
Long lines not properly shielded and terminated can cause receiver interference
Horizontal waveguide runs: slope slightly downward at the elbow
Drill a small drain hole in the elbow so condensed moisture drains out

onScreen: Z sub O set by construction
72 Ω line cut in half: each half still 72 Ω
Unshielded, unterminated long lines: receiver interference
Slope waveguide runs down at the elbow
Drain hole in the elbow
scenes.narration: Characteristic impedance depends only on how the line is built: conductor size, spacing and dielectric, which set L and C per unit length. It does not depend on length. Cut a 72 ohm line at its center, and each half still has a Z sub O of 72 ohms. If long transmission lines are not properly shielded and terminated, communications receiver interference might result: the line radiates and picks up stray RF, or radio frequency, energy, letting radar pulses leak into nearby receivers. Horizontal waveguide runs should slope slightly downward at the elbow, with a small drain hole drilled in the elbow, so condensed moisture drains out instead of pooling and causing loss, reflections and corrosion.

params.title: Keeping the PPI sweep in step

blocks.label: Radar antenna
blocks.note: Its position must reach the display

blocks.label: Synchro receiver
blocks.note: Angle arrives on stator lines S1, S2, S3

blocks.label: PPI sweep
blocks.note: Rotates in step with the antenna

onScreen: Antenna position must reach the display
Synchro transmitter geared to the antenna
Angle carried on stator lines S1, S2, S3
PPI sweep rotates in step
Both rotors share the AC reference
scenes.narration: The PPI, or plan position indicator, sweep must indicate the antenna position, and the two are frequently kept in synchronization by synchro systems. A synchro transmitter is geared to the antenna, and it drives a synchro receiver at the display. On a basic synchro system, the angular information is carried on the stator lines: the 3 leads, S1, S2 and S3, wired between the 2 units. The receiver turns the PPI sweep in step with the antenna. Meanwhile, both rotors share the same AC, or alternating current, reference.

params.title: Synchro transmitter vs. resolver
rows: For the exam: 2 windings (leads R1, R2)
Angle voltages on the stator lines
Sine and cosine of the antenna angle

onScreen: Synchro transmitter, for the exam: 2 rotor and 3 stator windings
Rotor leads R1, R2; stators S1, S2, S3 at 120°
Resolver: 1 rotor, 2 stator windings 90° apart
Resolver outputs sine and cosine
scenes.narration: For the exam, an antenna synchro transmitter is keyed as having 2 rotor and 3 stator windings. AC excitation enters the rotor through 2 leads, R1 and R2, and 3 stator windings, S1, S2 and S3, spaced 120 degrees apart, pick up the angle voltages. Strictly, a standard synchro's rotor is 1 winding with those 2 leads, but on the exam, choose 2 rotor and 3 stator windings. The basic resolver contains a rotor winding and 2 stator windings that are 90 degrees apart. As the rotor turns, the stator voltages vary as the sine and cosine of the antenna angle.

params.title: Sending antenna direction to the display
items: All ARPAs and radar systems must send the antenna direction to the display
Resolvers are the most common in modern radars: easy to convert to digital

onScreen: Every ARPA and radar sends antenna direction to the display
3-phase synchros
2-phase resolvers
Optical encoders
Resolvers: most common in modern radars
scenes.narration: Radar antenna direction must be sent to the display in all ARPAs, or automatic radar plotting aids, and in all radar systems. Any of these can do it: 3-phase synchros, 2-phase resolvers, or optical encoders. Resolvers are the most common type of antenna position indicating device in modern radars, because their sine and cosine outputs convert easily to digital bearing data.

blocks.label: Waveguide
blocks.note: Skin effect: currents on the inner walls

onScreen: 2-wire line
Supported by ¼-wave shorted stubs
Countless stubs merge into a closed box
Waveguide: skin effect keeps currents on the inner walls
scenes.narration: Where does waveguide theory come from? Picture a 2-wire line. Support it with quarter-wave shorted stubs. Add countless stubs, and they merge into a closed box: a waveguide. Skin effect keeps the currents on its inner walls. So waveguide theory is based on the principles of skin effect and the use of quarter-wave stubs. It is also based upon the movement of an electromagnetic field. The energy travels as a wave reflecting between the walls, which confine and guide the field. It is not current flow through conductive wires.

params.title: Microwave transmission lines
rows: Center conductor between parallel ground planes
Conductor over a single ground plane
Lower loss; costs more, harder to install

onScreen: Coax: more loss at microwave
Stripline: center conductor between 2 ground planes
Microstrip: only 1 ground plane
Waveguide: brass, aluminum or copper; lowest loss
scenes.narration: Here's how microwave lines compare. Ordinary coax has more loss at microwave frequencies. Stripline is a center conductor suspended between parallel conductive ground planes: 2 ground planes. Microstrip, by contrast, has only 1 ground plane. Waveguides can be constructed from brass, aluminum or copper, all good conductors that keep wall resistance low. At radar microwave frequencies, a waveguide is used because it has lower transmission losses than the other feedline types, even though it costs more and is harder to install.

callouts.label: J-hook: a thin wire bent into a small J-shaped loop
The loop links the magnetic field
Removes the signal from a magnetron or a waveguide
It's a J-hook, not a T-hook

onScreen: J-hook: thin wire bent into a J
Links the magnetic field
Removes the signal from a magnetron or waveguide
J-hook, not T-hook
scenes.narration: How is the signal taken out? With a thin wire called a J-hook: a small loop bent into the shape of a J. The loop links the magnetic field, so energy couples into it. A J-hook removes the signal from a magnetron, or from a waveguide. On the exam, it's a J-hook, not a T-hook.

params.title: Up to the antenna: the rotary joint

blocks.label: Rotary joint
blocks.note: One half turns against the other

blocks.label: Rotating slotted array
blocks.note: Radiates the beam as it turns

onScreen: Transceiver
Fixed waveguide run: bend radius over 2 inches
Rotary joint: stationary guide to rotating array
Rotating slotted array
scenes.narration: Let's follow the pulse up to the antenna. It leaves the transceiver and travels through the fixed waveguide run. Any right-angle bend in an X-band waveguide must have a radius greater than 2 inches, following the rule of thumb of at least 2 wavelengths, so the bend doesn't cause reflections. Then comes the rotary joint. It connects the stationary waveguide to the rotating antenna array. One half turns against the other, while the microwave energy passes through with little loss or leakage.

params.title: Why waveguide beats coax at microwave
rows: Small center conductor and its dielectric
The inner surface of the walls
Large surface spreads current: very small

onScreen: Coax loses energy in its center conductor and dielectric
Waveguide: large inner surface, very small I²R loss
Waveguide: considerably less loss at microwave
scenes.narration: Why are waveguides used instead of conventional coaxial transmission lines at microwave frequencies? Coax loses energy in its small center conductor and in its dielectric. A waveguide's resistive losses are very small, because its inner surface is large. The current spreads out over that surface, so the I squared R loss stays small. The result: at microwave frequencies, waveguides have considerably less loss than coax, so they're used instead.

params.title: Fields and coupling in a waveguide
items: Magnetic field: strongest at the edges, where the wall currents flow
Dominant TE<sub>10</sub> mode: the electric field peaks at the center
Insert or extract RF with a voltage probe, a current loop or an aperture window

onScreen: Magnetic field strongest at the edges
TE sub 10 mode: electric field peaks at the center
Voltage probe, current loop or aperture window
Not coupling capacitance
scenes.narration: Inside a waveguide, the magnetic field is strongest at the edges, where the wall currents flow. In the dominant T E sub one zero mode, the electric field peaks at the center. To insert RF energy into a waveguide, or extract it, you can use a voltage probe, a current loop or an aperture window. Coupling capacitance is not used, so on the exam, that's the one that would not be used.
